doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Learning beyond books; practicing at Xavier; older musicians' love
summary: Printed music is a base to make your own; Clifford Brown's classical approach, and nuns objecting to Monk at Xavier practice rooms.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Which there are an awful lot of books now, aren’t there?

Oh yeah, a lot of books man. There weren’t any books like that when I was coming up on how to — now there are a lot of books but that could serve you well if you know how to use them. But at some point you have to get away from the book. You have to take the knowledge in the book and turn it inside out. Like today, and I’ve always taught, about printed music. Printed music has the function of being able to play from the top of the music all the way down, no mistakes, understand everything about the rhythm, the phrasing, the dynamics, everything about it. Okay that’s one thing. The next thing from printed music, you can take things out of the content and make them your own, just what’s written already. And I found myself doing that as a young musician and at the time I didn’t know how valuable it was because I used to play out of those exercise books I was talking about. And before I started really trying to improvise I used to play all the exercises straight down you know. And then when I started listening to more jazz, people like Clifford Brown and Miles, I would play something out of the exercise books and I’d get to one little phrase and it would sound like — hey that sounds like something Clifford Brown would use or play because he had that classical background. He played jazz but his jazz were classical solos, the way he approached the trumpet. So I’d find myself taking a measure or phrase and in fifteen, twenty minutes I’m working it in and out trying it inside out and all of a sudden, oh wait a minute, I’ve got to get back to the book. But later on I’d finally say wow, that was very valuable. Nobody told me to do that because when I went to school man you couldn’t really play jazz in the practice rooms. I’m sure that was happening all over the country. I went to Xavier University and the practice rooms when I was trying to play a Thelonious Monk thing on the piano and every time I hit the tritone the nuns would knock on the door, “Mr. Kerr, now, this is for serious music, you can’t play that here.” I said, “Well sister, I’m serious.” You know but it was
like that. You couldn’t do that man. But even teaching in the jazz like I wound up doing, I didn’t go to school for that but my school was out there, doing it.
Right. And a student is lucky to have someone who’s been out there. That’s what I think anyway.

Exactly man. You know like the older musicians who were in my living room when I was a kid. As I grew up and got older and started going out there they treated me with the same love that my dad gave to them.
